topic.title: The sample flat is built to lie politely
topic.claim: A sample flat isn't a preview of your home; it's a set, built so small rooms look big.
topic.moment: Walking through a show flat with soft lights, a narrow bed and no wardrobe doors open.

turn.believed: The sample flat shows what you'll get.
turn.actually: Furniture is chosen and placed to hide how tight the rooms are.

topic.because: You decide with your eyes, not a tape measure. A builder only needs you to feel space for ten minutes.
topic.payoff: Carry a tape. Measure where your own double bed would go. That's the real flat.
topic.behaviour: Buyers fall for staged flats; builders style them with slim furniture and mirrors.
topic.mechanism: A feeling of space sells faster than square feet on paper.
topic.group: First-time flat buyers in their late 20s and 30s
topic.send_to: The friend who just booked a flat after one site visit.
topic.why_now: Festive launches and 'Diwali offers' bring a wave of site visits.

mechanism.broken_premise: None fails outright. The weakest one is premise 2, which treats the token cheque as the point of commitment and says the buyer could not have measured. Under RERA Section 13(1) a promoter can't take more than 10% of the price before a registered written agreement for sale. Section 2(k) defines carpet area as a legal measure that must be disclosed. Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) regulators such as UP RERA tell buyers to rely on it. So the token cheque is a small and often partly recoverable step, and the dimensions are on paper before the binding agreement. The buyer skipped the measuring, but it was possible. The post also leaves out a real remedy: Section 12 names 'model apartment' next to adverts, so if the sample flat makes a false statement, the buyer can get compensation or withdraw with full refund plus interest. That is a gap in the take, not a refutation.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Sample flats are designed as sales tools. Long-running Indian buyer guidance describes smaller-than-standard beds and cupboards, designer lighting, missing internal doors, glass or gypsum partitions and sometimes higher ceilings, all of which make a room feel bigger than the bare shell you get. What legally binds the developer isn't the show flat but the RERA carpet area (Section 2(k)) and the floor plan in the registered agreement for sale. Before that agreement, the promoter can't take more than 10% (Section 13(1)). If the model apartment itself misrepresents the unit, Section 12 lets the buyer claim compensation or withdraw with full refund plus interest. Furniture that is legitimately downsized isn't a 'false statement', though, so checking the disclosed room dimensions against your own furniture is the buyer's job, which is the post's point.

sources.quote: Where any person makes an advance or a deposit on the basis of the information contained in the notice, advertisement or prospectus, or on the basis of any model apartment, plot or building, as the case may be, and sustains any loss or damage by reason of any incorrect, false statement included therein, he shall be compensated by the promoter

A promoter shall not accept a sum more than ten per cent of the cost of the apartment, plot, or building ... [without first entering into a registered written agreement for sale]; "carpet area" means the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by the external walls

mechanism.broken_premise: The staging premise holds and so does the conclusion. Two supporting claims are wrong or overstated. (1) 'You never had a number' and 'the tape measure comes out after the cheque': under RERA a registered project must disclose and sell on carpet area, which Section 2(k) defines as 'net usable floor area'. Section 13 also caps the advance at 10% of the cost until a written agreement for sale is signed, and that agreement states the carpet area. So the buyer is given a number before they are fully committed, and the token is a small, limited advance, not the moment the money is lost. What the buyer usually lacks is room-by-room dimensions and a furniture plan, not a total area. (2) 'Same square feet as the sample': this cannot be assumed. Sample flats are often built with thinner walls, higher ceilings or doors removed, so they may not match the real unit's dimensions at all. That adds to the post's point, but the line is wrong as written.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Show flats are marketing displays, and sources describe the same tricks: furniture kept smaller so rooms look bigger, mirrors and glass, thinner walls and higher ceilings than the real flat. Showing one is legal and makes no binding promise about how the space feels. The legal protection is the RERA carpet-area figure, which is the basis of sale, must appear in the agreement for sale (signed before more than 10% is paid) and gets a refund if the built area comes up short. That figure is a total floor area, so it tells you nothing about whether your own bed, wardrobe swing and door clearances fit. Buyers have to check that against the room dimensions on the floor plan or with a tape measure in the real unit.

[cover] A sample flat isn't a preview of your home, it's [a set]
Built to feel big for the ten minutes you're inside.
 

[slide 1] A sample flat isn't a preview of your home, it's a set.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's a Sunday in October. A Diwali offer banner at the gate, blue shoe covers on your feet, the sales guy holding the door.
The bedroom has a neat bed, a little narrower than the one you sleep on. A tall mirror covers one wall. The wardrobe doors stay shut the whole visit.

[slide 3] It feels huge. Much bigger than your PG room. You step onto the balcony and shoot a slow video for the family group.
Everyone replies with the same word: "Spacious." By the weekend, the token cheque is signed.

[slide 4] Try to remember one number from that room. You can't. You never had one.
That narrow bed left extra floor showing, and the mirror made one wall look like two. Those shut wardrobe doors never had to swing into anything.
The builder only needs ten minutes of you feeling space. The tape measure comes out after the cheque.

[slide 5] Possession day. Bare walls, one bulb hanging from the ceiling. Your own double bed comes in, wider than the neat one in the sample, and touches the wall on one side.
You pull the wardrobe door. It stops halfway, against your mattress.
Same square feet as the sample. They just never put your bed in it.

[end card] Open it again before your next site visit, with a tape measure in your bag.
The friend who just booked a flat after one site visit.

[caption] The most honest thing in any sample flat is the tape measure you forgot to bring.

[alt text] A five-slide carousel. The cover reads: A sample flat isn't a preview of your home, it's a set. The slides follow a reader on a festive-season site visit. The show flat has a bed a little narrower than theirs, a tall mirror on one wall, and wardrobe doors that stay shut. It feels spacious, the family group agrees, and the token cheque is signed. The reader realises they never measured anything: the narrow bed left floor showing, the mirror doubled a wall, and the shut wardrobe never had to open. On possession day their own wider double bed touches the wall and the wardrobe door stops halfway against the mattress. The point is that the sample flat sells ten minutes of feeling space, and the real flat is the one your own bed goes into.

cover.sub: Built to feel big for the ten minutes you're inside.

paragraphs: A sample flat isn't a preview of your home, it's a set.
slides.why_swipe: A set for what, and who was it built for?

paragraphs: It's a Sunday in October. A Diwali offer banner at the gate, blue shoe covers on your feet, the sales guy holding the door.
The bedroom has a neat bed, a little narrower than the one you sleep on. A tall mirror covers one wall. The wardrobe doors stay shut the whole visit.
slides.why_swipe: So how does that room make you feel?

paragraphs: It feels huge. Much bigger than your PG room. You step onto the balcony and shoot a slow video for the family group.
Everyone replies with the same word: "Spacious." By the weekend, the token cheque is signed.
slides.why_swipe: What did you actually check before signing?

paragraphs: Try to remember one number from that room. You can't. You never had one.
That narrow bed left extra floor showing, and the mirror made one wall look like two. Those shut wardrobe doors never had to swing into anything.
**The builder only needs ten minutes of you feeling space. The tape measure comes out after the cheque.**
slides.why_swipe: So what happens when your own things move in?

paragraphs: Possession day. Bare walls, one bulb hanging from the ceiling. Your own double bed comes in, wider than the neat one in the sample, and touches the wall on one side.
You pull the wardrobe door. It stops halfway, against your mattress.
**Same square feet as the sample. They just never put your bed in it.**

end.save: Open it again before your next site visit, with a tape measure in your bag.
end.send: The friend who just booked a flat after one site visit.
end.promise: How things really get sold to you.

draft.caption: The most honest thing in any sample flat is the tape measure you forgot to bring.
draft.alt_text: A five-slide carousel. The cover reads: A sample flat isn't a preview of your home, it's a set. The slides follow a reader on a festive-season site visit. The show flat has a bed a little narrower than theirs, a tall mirror on one wall, and wardrobe doors that stay shut. It feels spacious, the family group agrees, and the token cheque is signed. The reader realises they never measured anything: the narrow bed left floor showing, the mirror doubled a wall, and the shut wardrobe never had to open. On possession day their own wider double bed touches the wall and the wardrobe door stops halfway against the mattress. The point is that the sample flat sells ten minutes of feeling space, and the real flat is the one your own bed goes into.
